It is not permitted to pour dichromate down the sink, it is really a quite toxic material as it is a real flora and fauna killer. 

 But you can kill it's toxicity by chucking it into a container with your old developer solutions. That instantly converts it to an insoluble sludge of basic CrIII compounds. Don't put a lid back on the container tightly though as CO2 gas needs to come off from your carbonate and acid reaction.

[/b]

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: Thank you Jeff, I will start to do that right away. I can reuse dichromate baths for so long I have just stored the used chemical. Now I have aquired about a gallon of the stuff. I have to replace me developer every session so I have lots of extra to use.

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.content_md:
> **Colin Kaminski:** Thank you Jeff, I will start to do that right away. I can reuse dichromate baths for so long I have just stored the used chemical. Now I have aquired about a gallon of the stuff. I have to replace me developer every session so I have lots of extra to use.

You do need to make sure your developer is in great excess over the dichromate Colin , so don't pour dev into old dichromate but dichromate into **plenty** of old dev.

I say this because although I never myself on principle use any developers that contain sulfite (eg D19 ) if such developers get turned to acid then you can get SO2 coming off. That will not happen as long as everything stays very alkaline. 

Jeff

posts.author: Gary Deal
posts.content_md:
Thanks Jeff, so my "Toxic Sludge Bucket" isn't as toxic as I'd thought? It's got plenty of used developer(s) and stop bath, some fixer, and some dichromate rinse water. And whatever else I don't think I should be tossing down the drain or just feel like dumping in the bucket. I'd probably notice any SO2 coming off, it's scent-free. I suppose a big scoop of carbonate or some lye would keep it plenty alkaline against whatever acetic I pour in.

At the risk of enlarging this "one liner" section, that makes me wonder about that "insoluble sludge of basic CrIII compounds". Does this then mean that there's a developable material in the emulsion when the reversal bleach hasn't been completely cleared? And since we've been speaking of hardening occurring because of that bleach, would it follow that at some point in the rinse cycle there's substantially more in the hardened areas than in the non-hardened areas? If so, what are the characteristics of the CrIII compounds and would it be advantageous to some process to develop those in place? As an aside, isn't a sulfite "clearing bath" used to remove the dichromate stain? What are the chemical results of that?
